title: Levi Todd, Lexington Co-Founder
summary: Levi Todd (1756–1807) helped lay out Lexington’s stockade, became Kentucky County’s first clerk, and later served decades as Fayette County clerk.
bodyMarkdown:
[Levi Todd](/people/#levi-todd) (1756–1807) was born in Pennsylvania and raised in Virginia, where he studied law. In 1775 he came out to Kentucky with his brothers [John](/people/#john-todd) and Robert. They were part of the first wave of settlers in the Bluegrass.

That year a party of hunters camped at a spring in the Bluegrass heard of the first fighting of the Revolution and named the spot Lexington, after the Massachusetts battle. The story of [how Lexington got its name](/stories/lexington-named/) tells that part. In 1779 [Robert Patterson](/people/#robert-patterson) led the men who built a blockhouse and stockade there, and the town grew from it. Levi Todd helped lay out the stockade and was one of the town's first trustees.

When Virginia made Kentucky a county of its own in 1776, Todd became the first clerk of [Kentucky County](https://grokipedia.com/page/Kentucky_County,_Virginia), in 1777. He kept the court records, land entries, and deeds, the paper on which the whole frontier ran.

He also fought. Todd went with [George Rogers Clark](/people/#george-rogers-clark) on the [Illinois campaign](https://grokipedia.com/page/Illinois_campaign) and was there when Clark took Kaskaskia on July 4, 1778.

In August 1782 Native and British forces besieged [Bryan Station](/stories/bryan-station-siege-august-1782/). Todd led about forty men from Lexington to help. Days later he fought at the [Battle of Blue Licks](/stories/battle-of-blue-licks/), where his brother [Col. John Todd](/stories/col-john-todd-of-lexington/) was killed. Levi Todd wrote one of the earliest official accounts of the defeat.

After Fayette County was formed in 1780, Todd served as its clerk for decades. He rose to major general of the Kentucky militia. He built Ellerslie, said to be Fayette County's first brick house, and married Jane Briggs. Their son Robert Smith Todd became the father of [Mary Todd Lincoln](/people/#mary-todd-lincoln), which made Levi Todd the grandfather of a First Lady.

He died in 1807 and was buried in Fayette County.

## Kentucky today

The Mary Todd Lincoln House on West Main Street in Lexington tells the Todd family story. Many early Fayette County deeds and court records still carry Levi Todd's hand as clerk.
